works.title: Fixed shot pool
works.line: Make different films from one locked inventory of shots.
works.thesis: Make the audience infer a different cause or motive from identical raw images. The defining cut changes what an encounter means while every visible source image remains traceable to the same frozen pool.
works.state: ◻(ShotAsset) has asset_id, source hash, native frame bounds, and source anchor. ◻(PictureEdit) is an ordered list of asset_id, in/out frame, integer output duration, direction, and speed. ◻(SoundEdit) has separately versioned tracks, cues, and offsets. Shot pool × edit → [render] → ◻(Screening).
works.invariant: Freeze one asset manifest before branching. Every visible frame must resolve to a declared asset and valid source range. Permit timing, order, repeat, omission, reverse, and independent audio changes. Keep geometry, color, content, and framing of every referenced image fixed for this exercise.
works.proof: Shoot or draw eight short originals: a clock, a hand with a parcel, a second hand, a door, a glance, a dropped receipt, a person exiting, and an empty threshold. Make a 20–30 second ordinary handoff and a second cut that makes the parcel seem illicit. Screen once with one shared sound bed, then with both final mixes. The historical count is 42. Eight is this proof’s budget.
works.fixture: A=[clock, hand, door, exit] and B=[exit, door, hand, clock] pass inventory membership on the same pool hash. A generated insert or an out-of-bounds source frame fails. Audio-only replacement must preserve the serialized picture edit.
works.critic: Ask for the perceived cause, the person acting on it, and the exact cut or audible cue that changed the inference. Report whether each cut reads at normal speed and whether the distinction survives the common-sound screening.

works.title: Second-person voice

works.line: Let a voice say “you” while the image observes someone else.
works.thesis: Make a spectator feel personally addressed while an anonymous figure stays available to observation. The proof hinges on one interval in which the voice’s address and the image’s point of view become perceptibly separate.

[bind] maps an address clause and an observed action to a declared relation: anticipates, overlaps, lags, or leaves silence.
works.invariant: Keep narrative address in the second person in the constrained language. Quoted diegetic speech lives on its own track. Preserve the declared addressee until a marked shift. Keep a voice-free passage long enough for the spectator to notice the body or place on its own.
works.proof: Build 35 seconds: a person wakes, ignores a ringing telephone, and takes an identical staircase twice. Keep the camera outside their viewpoint. Record two original second-person tracks with identical words, one ahead of actions and one delayed. Leave a held shot with only room sound.

works.proof: Make two 25-second movements around a fictional or consented closed rail station: an empty platform plus a dated trace, then two accounts of the last train that disagree about a detail. works.thesis: Turn an industrial dependency into a visual and audible discovery. Hold a product long enough to make its shape familiar, then cut to the process or negative form that explains how it came into being.
works.state: ◻(ProcessStep) has process_id, named inputs and outputs, material evidence, and source anchor. ◻(ReverseTour) traverses an evidenced path from output toward prerequisites. ◻(VerseLine) has spoken text, scansion, caesura, stress/cue timing, and associated step ID.
works.invariant: Follow declared process edges in reverse dependency order. Separate industrial process order from whether a shot runs forward or backward. works.proof: Make a 25–40 second reverse tour from a cast key or a user-supplied object. Place one cut on a caesura and one against it to test the effect.

works.title: Visual slapstick from verbal play
works.line: Carry a verbal joke into a cut, a gesture, or the street itself.
works.thesis: Make a child or trickster’s goal simple enough to survive a city that keeps changing the terms of the chase. Translate a linguistic ambiguity into a physical setup and a filmic payoff.
works.state: ◻(Gag) has goal, setup prop, conventional expectation, reversal, and recovery beat. ◻(Route) is a graph of entrances, exits, obstacles, and match anchors. ◻(GagOperation) changes screen time, screen direction, object identity, or apparent place under a declared exception.
works.invariant: Preserve the protagonist’s objective and a recognizable anchor at every discontinuous cut. Each effect introduces a specific reversal with a consequence. Keep a clean continuity cut as the reference for comparing comic timing.
works.proof: Make a 20-second pursuit of a bus, train, or other promised vehicle. Use three city locations and one prop that gets reinterpreted twice. Test a jump cut for impossible distance and a match cut that turns a queue into an obstacle. Start with the same straightforward chase.
works.fixture: Setup A establishes who wants the vehicle. Cut B breaks distance while keeping the vehicle or prop identifiable. Removing the recognizable match anchor makes B an intentional negative control. A gag with no downstream event consequence fails the beat contract.
works.critic: With sound off, have a viewer state the goal and locate the moment each joke turns. Replay with sound and see whether impact, pause, or offscreen cue improves the timing.
works.shared: Make the visitor’s goal legible before introducing a running gag with the envelope and signs. Keep the door closed and make the failed route itself the comic event.

works.line: Stage an ordinary relationship inside schedules, rules, and cramped space.

works.proof: Make a 35-second two-person encounter around a factory or service desk where co-workers must conceal a private commitment. They have one overlapping break and one doorway visible to a supervisor. Play the encounter under the original shift and a late bell that removes the safe window.

works.title: Interested confession
works.byline: René Clément · dialogue by Raymond Queneau · 1954
works.line: Cut between what a speaker claims, what happened, and what a listener hears.
works.thesis: Make a confession operate as a present-tense action. Give the speaker a reason to retell the past and the listener enough evidence to make a different inference. Distinguish what a flashback establishes from what the speaker wants it to establish.
works.state: ◻(Claim) has claim_id, speaker, target listener, asserted event, desired effect, and timeline position. ◻(SceneEvidence) has evidence_id, event relation, perspective, and level of certainty. ◻(ListenerState) holds what the listener can hear, see, infer, or withhold.
works.invariant: Preserve an event ledger independent of each telling. Mark recollected images as a perspective unless an independent scene or material trace supports them. Each pivotal line has a listener consequence that can be staged and inspected.
works.proof: Make a 30–45 second encounter in which a visitor claims they returned a borrowed object. Cut to a version of the return that hides one consequential gesture. Give the listener a receipt, a look, or an audible clue that can change what they decide to do next.
works.fixture: Claim C1 may conflict with E2 while both records survive. A spoken line and a flashback derive from distinct entries. A cut that presents E2 as verified while E2 is a subjective reconstruction fails.
works.critic: Ask what the speaker wants now, what the listener believes, and which cut, look, or clause changed the balance. Run two viewers on alternate reaction placements if possible.
works.shared: The visitor recounts what happened at the bench to persuade a listener that the envelope was left untouched. Keep the seed event ledger and give the listener one independent clue.

Declared on screen: the 1942 sitters play fictional roles; box, receipt and silhouettes are props.

works.line: Put a group under pressure and let one strange object redirect its choices.
works.thesis: Earn a surreal detail by placing it inside a concrete survival or escape problem. The detail should change a decision, relationship, or allocation while the setting retains physical resistance.
works.state: ◻(WorldState) records routes, resource stock, supports, obstacles, and positions. ◻(GroupDecision) records chooser, alternatives, resource costs, and resulting allegiances. ◻(Interruption) has first appearance, material affordance, rule exception if any, and next consequence.
works.invariant: Conserve resources and track location and possession across cuts. Declare the scope of any impossible behavior. Tie the strange detail to an action the group can take and a state that persists after it.
works.proof: Stage 30–45 seconds of three people crossing a flooded passage with one dry bag and one safe plank. An immaculate wedding shoe floats into reach. One person retrieves it and the group has to change its crossing order. Make an alternate in which the interruption stays visually identical but lands earlier.
works.fixture: If the plank holds one person, simultaneous occupancy fails unless the scenario explicitly changes the material law. A retrieved object gains a holder and changes the next available action. A disappeared possession without a logged event fails continuity.

works.title: Rotating type and apparent depth
works.byline: Marcel Duchamp, with Man Ray and Marc Allégret · 1926
works.line: Alternate optical depth with words that demand to be read.
works.thesis: Make one flat mechanism produce two acts of attention. The first disc seems to move in depth. The next makes the eye pursue a sentence around a surface. Use the moment of switching between them as the principal event.
works.state: ◻(Disc) has kind, radius, graphic source, turn direction, and angular velocity curve. ◻(GlyphPath) maps character order to radius, angle, and tangent. ◻(ExposureSequence) alternates disc types using an integer frame clock. [project] maps planar marks to a frame.
works.invariant: Keep the geometry on a flat plane for the proof. Preserve glyph order under rotation and keep the two disc kinds legible. Make the release motion safe to inspect, with predictable playback and a still or reduced-motion view when the result is interactive.
works.proof: Make 18–25 seconds with two original optical discs and two original text discs. One seems to expand toward the eye and one recedes. Then make one reading disc legible at its chosen speed. Offer a still pass to distinguish legibility of layout from the effect of movement.

works.title: Long-form panel palindrome
works.line: Reverse a comic’s panel sequence after its midpoint.
works.thesis: Make a familiar drawing acquire a second function when its neighbors arrive in reverse order. Build a hinge that makes the reversal feel earned across page turns.
works.state: ◻(Panel) has immutable artwork ID, lettered text, speaker, and visual anchors. ◻(ReadingOrder) stores the ordered panel IDs across pages. ◻(StoryRole) maps each occurrence to its local purpose and causal neighbors. [mirror] maps the chosen prefix into a suffix by reverse order.
works.invariant: Every mirrored occurrence points to the exact original panel and lettering. Declare whether the work uses a single hinge panel or a seam between paired panels. Page grids may change with format while the flattened panel order remains identical.
works.proof: Make a four-page original story with nine unique panels and one of those as the hinge. Use the other eight panels on either side, yielding 17 occurrences. Begin with an action that reads as accusation and returns as protection. Place the hinge on a purposeful page turn.
works.fixture: [A,B,C,X,C,B,A] passes a single-center check. [A,B,C,X,C,B′,A] fails when B′ changes the balloon or drawing. Validate normalized content IDs and flattened reading order after every export.
works.critic: Have someone read at normal pace without the symmetry key, then point to the turning panel and explain which repeated drawing means something different. Check the payoff at phone and print size.
works.shared: Make a forward passage through the station beats, then repeat the exact panel IDs in reverse. Treat the backward leg as a second reading of the evidence. Keep the shared incident in canonical chronological order outside the page.

The hinge X, the bell that can only be rung from behind the service door, opens page 3 after a page turn. The porter's opening shout reads as an accusation; when the same panel closes the story it reads as protection. Voices are captions with synthesized murmurs, and each repeated panel reuses the same murmur.

works.title: A short palindrome with a hinge
works.line: Use one line as the hinge that flips an argument.
works.thesis: Build a tight conversational reversal in which the same speech and drawings change who seems to be on the defensive. The central line pivots the exchange within one page.
works.state: ◻(ExchangePanel) binds an immutable visual asset to speaker and balloon text. ◻(SpeechAct) assigns each occurrence a local function such as accuse, deny, reassure, or concede. ◻(Hinge) is the single permitted unpaired occurrence.
works.invariant: Mirror the complete sequence of story panels around the hinge, preserving art and words. Title and page furniture live outside the mirrored sequence. Record how the pragmatic meaning changes through adjacency alone.
works.proof: Draw one page of seven occurrences: three panels, one hinge, the same three in reverse. Two people dispute who left a note. Make the hinge reveal that the note was meant for the person accusing the other. Repeat the art and lettering exactly.
works.fixture: [A,B,C,H,C,B,A] passes. Swapping speakers on the second B or reversing the letters within a balloon fails. Two different hinges with the same pair sequence are legal separate candidates.
works.critic: After one natural reading, ask which line shifted the leverage and which repeated line changed meaning. Judge that change before pointing out the symmetry.
works.shared: Let two people ask who left the key. Build three exact panel pairs and a hinge in which the key’s ownership is questioned. The observed station facts remain the same.

works.work: 99 Ways to Tell a Story · Subjective
works.title: First-person reconstruction
works.line: Retell the same incident through what one participant can perceive.
works.thesis: Keep one event sequence while making the audience inhabit a character’s restricted information. Let hands, gaze direction, and offscreen speech do the work a wide shot did in the baseline.
works.state: ◻(Event) has objective identity and order. ◻(EyePose) has position, direction, and field of view. ◻(Observation) has event_id, sensory channel, evidence, and access condition. [observe] maps shared events and eye pose into the character’s visible and audible world.
works.invariant: Hold canonical participants, causality, and outcome fixed. Every visible object must be accessible from the chosen viewpoint. Handle outside-view events with a permitted sensory cue, inference, or uncertainty. Mark reflective glimpses as geometrically supported.
works.proof: Redraw a six-panel household anecdote through the main character’s eyes. Preserve its initial errand and failed outcome. Provide one unseen interruption through sound or a speech balloon and one visible object that only enters after a head turn.
works.fixture: If an object lies outside a pose’s field of view, omit it until a turn or supported reflection. Keep the original event ID even when the spectator learns it indirectly. A disembodied reverse shot fails strict viewpoint mode.
works.critic: Ask what the spectator knew before the turn, which cue changed that knowledge, and whether the endpoint still matches the baseline. Compare without giving the viewer the shot list first.
works.shared: Redraw the station incident through the visitor’s eyes. The bell comes from offscreen. Hands open the envelope. Keep the closed door and the final placement of the key clear.
works.notes: The same office incident (events E1 to E5 from 99-ways-template) redrawn through the clerk's eyes. The film opens on the clerk's own hands on the desk and the note "Fetch the service key!" The question "What time is it?" comes from a balloon whose tail leaves the frame, with a murmur panned hard left. The wall clock appears only in panel 3, after a head turn drawn with motion lines. The hands then open the cupboard and lift empty in front of the keys, and the service key stays on its hook. The film ends with the objective and subjective pages side by side. The clock's tick is heard before it is seen.

works.line: Show what each invention makes possible through motion and consequence.
works.thesis: Make a machine’s problem intelligible through performance. Each change in mechanism must visibly alter what a body, wheel, or material can do. Let narration complicate that action with a joke or observation.

works.line: Turn a brief, prompt, workflow, or tool into a system instruction that can direct real production.

works.title: Combinatorial lines and a lipogram
works.line: Write interchangeable lines, then measure what survives a forbidden letter.
works.thesis: Write one event as a family of texts. Every legal assembly should preserve the incident and leave room for a distinct voice. Use the missing letter to discover which facts are hardest to name.
works.state: ◻(Slot) has a position, event ID, grammar, and three candidate lines. ◻(Combination) has one line ID per slot. [assemble] yields a text. [exclude letter] restricts the admissible IDs in each slot.
works.invariant: Keep event order and outcomes fixed. Write six slots with three distinct lines per slot. Any line must fit its slot beside every other slot’s choices. Freeze the line bank before applying the secondary lipogram.
works.proof: Make a six-line incident with three alternatives per line and show two sharply different assemblies. Apply a declared letter ban to the frozen bank and show two surviving texts. Report 3⁶ = 729 possible ID combinations before filtering and the actual survivor count afterward.
works.fixture: Use the letter E, case-insensitive and with accents folded. Count the product of surviving choices per slot and verify it by enumeration. Aim for at least one survivor in every slot and two choices in one slot. In a negative test, add an É to a candidate and check that it is excluded.
works.critic: Read the samples without their IDs. Check that each delivers the same six facts and has a recognizable voice. Verify the character rule on the assembled text and inspect the slot with the fewest alternatives.
works.shared: Give E01 through E06 one line each. For the lipogram, try a brass bit cut to fit a lock for E04 and a plank for sitting for E05, then test whether the objects still read clearly.

works.title: One solution, two clue orders
works.byline: Ouvroir de littérature policière potentielle · Detective fiction
works.line: Permute the evidence in a locked-room mystery and count the explanations still possible.
works.thesis: Let clue order guide suspicion while the same evidence determines the answer. A fair mystery rewards a reader who tracks which account each observation rules out.
works.state: ◻(Hypothesis) pairs a suspect with an access method. ◻(Clue) cites an observable fact and has a truth value under every hypothesis. ◻(Reveal) orders clue IDs. [intersect] gives the candidates still compatible with the revealed evidence.
works.invariant: Freeze the room rules, culprit, method, evidence wording, and final clue. Every scheduled clue is true of the solution. Two readings use the same evidence and differ in the order of the earlier clues.
works.proof: Write two short versions of a sealed-room or sealed-container puzzle. Show the reader where they can pause and solve it before opening the answer. Publish the surviving-set trace after each clue in each version.
works.fixture: Start with A, B, and C and two methods per suspect. One early clue rules out method 2 and one rules out C. Reveal these in either order, leaving A and B using method 1. The last clue must exclude B through an observable detail available to the reader.
works.critic: Check that the two openings create different plausible suspicions, the final answer follows from shown facts, and a second valid answer or unstated access route would fail the proof.
works.shared: Use the closed service door as a constraint on who could have placed the brass key inside the envelope before E03. Keep the visitor’s later actions and the public station record fixed.

works.title: Fibonacci montage
works.line: Cut the same six shots twice under an exact frame-count score.
works.thesis: Give editorial attention a measurable price in frames. Reassign who gets the longest look by changing where a shot sits in the edit.
works.state: ◻(Shot) has a source ID, first frame, usable range, and an action anchor. ◻(Cut) is a permutation of six IDs. [score position] assigns an exact output duration and [trim] takes that many contiguous source frames.
works.invariant: Use one frozen inventory of six shots, each exactly once per edit. Positions take 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, and 89 frames at 24 fps. Use straight cuts and a fixed in-point with 89 usable frames per shot. Keep the same ambience bed and any short sync cues attached to their source shots.
works.proof: Make a chronological cut and a second version that opens on a consequence. Export both in constant frame rate with edit lists showing source ranges and cumulative output frames. Each shot needs an action cue legible even in its shortest assigned window.
works.fixture: Use E01–E06 for the first order and E05, E01, E02, E03, E04, E06 for the second. Both exports contain exactly 220 frames. Intentionally export one 221-frame version to verify that the duration check catches a one-frame tail.
works.critic: Screen both cuts before looking at the edit lists. Mark where you first infer why the key sits on the bench. Check that every action ID remains legible and the final service-door state survives the trim.
works.shared: Start the second cut with the key landing on the bench, then show how it got there. Give the closing shot room to establish that the door stays shut.

works.title: Tile permutation and a forbidden hue
works.line: Change the composition by moving the same painted tiles across a grid.
works.thesis: Make adjacency create a figure that the individual tiles cannot supply. Reassemble the same inventory so a continuous form becomes a dispersed field.
works.state: ◻(Tile) has an ID, orientation, pigments, and motif mask. ◻(Canvas) is a bijection between sixteen tiles and a four-by-four grid. [permute] changes site assignments. [measure] finds orthogonally adjacent motif components.
works.invariant: Freeze sixteen equal tiles and their orientations. Declare one excluded hue group and the admissible swatches before painting. Every assembly displays each tile exactly once and keeps its pigments, marks, and orientation fixed.
works.proof: Arrange six marked tiles into one connected figure in assembly A. In assembly B disperse the same six so every connected component has at most two tiles. Show both canvases side by side and keep a photograph or source layer for every tile.
works.fixture: Use six amber-marked tiles and ten unmarked tiles with a palette that excludes blue. In rows 1–2 and columns 1–3 the six form one component. Pairs on r1c1–r1c2, r3c1–r3c2, and r4c3–r4c4 form three separate components.
works.critic: Inspect the frozen swatches and both tile manifests. Identify whether a viewer can trace the continuous motif in A and where the figure dissolves in B.
works.shared: Translate the closed door, key, and bench into paintable motifs. Let the brass color tie the fragments into a key shape in one arrangement and scatter it through the station in the other.

works.title: Grammatical mold, donor lexicon
works.byline: Atelier de littérature assistée par la mathématique et les ordinateurs · Paul Braffort and Jacques Roubaud
works.line: Build a runnable generator that puts one text’s vocabulary into another text’s grammar.
works.thesis: Make the mold and the dictionary independently inspectable so a reader can tell which text supplies the sentence shape and which supplies its verbal material.
works.state: ◻(Mold) alternates fixed text with typed slots. ◻(Lexeme) has a donor location, lemma, part of speech, inflections, and optional prosody. [solve with seed] selects a compatible filling and logs every choice.
works.invariant: Freeze the source mold, donor spans, slot types, and declared agreement rules. Preserve fixed words and punctuation. Every inserted lemma must come from the donor and every surface form must have a documented inflection. Report an unfillable slot explicitly.
works.proof: From an original source of two to four lines, remove content words at four or more typed positions. Build a tiny runnable generator and a closed, attributable donor lexicon. Return two distinct legal outputs, their fill traces, and a run that reproduces one output from its seed.
works.fixture: Use a mold with a singular noun that agrees with a present-tense verb, plus at least one adjective slot. Run three recorded seeds. Remove every compatible verb from the donor in a negative run and name the blocked slot in the failure report.
works.critic: Reconstruct each output from the mold and the trace. Check agreement, position, donor provenance, and any meter actually declared. Read both outputs and identify which change the new vocabulary makes audible.
works.shared: Keep the grammar of a short report of E01–E06. Fill it from an original list of nautical or astronomical words and trace any changes to the apparent setting.

works.title: A palindromic tasting menu
works.line: Mirror five cooking techniques around one course and leave an ingredient family out.
works.thesis: Let a technique recur with a different role in the meal. The last course should give the first a recognizable echo through texture or aroma.
works.state: ◻(Course) has a position, defining technique, sensory role, and ingredient tree. ◻(Menu) is an ordered course list. [mirror] pairs positions i and 6−i and [expand] resolves ingredients inside stocks, sauces, and garnishes.
works.invariant: Use five courses with technique sequence roast, steam, poach, steam, roast. Choose an excluded ingredient family up front. Apply it to all nested ingredients. Keep position pairs distinct as dishes while sharing the declared technique.
works.proof: Make a five-course menu with recipe cards, defining steps, an ingredient substitution ledger, and a common prep timeline. Make the center course change the direction of the sequence from opening to closing.
works.fixture: Exclude onion, garlic, leek, shallot, chive, and scallion for the exercise. Walk every sauce and stock to its base ingredients. Seed one stock containing onion to test rejection. Mark any opaque purchased ingredient as unverified.
works.critic: Check execution order, technique symmetry, and the full ingredient tree. Describe what the design predicts and record sensory judgments only for food actually tasted.
works.shared: Use the station’s opening, arrival, and departure as structural cues. Put a single revealing course in the center and echo the outer courses by technique.

works.title: A reversible stage score
works.line: Perform one cue score forward and back with an explicit inverse for each action.
works.thesis: Use the same score to make an arrival and an extraction. Give the reverse passage enough dramatic intent that an audience can follow what each performer wants.
works.state: ◻(StageState) tracks performer marks, prop locations, and resettable cues. ◻(Card) has a line or silence, a forward action, an inverse, and both preconditions. [play] applies a card in the declared direction and advances the state.
works.invariant: Freeze six cue cards, their words, and each inverse before rehearsal. Forward order is 1 through 6. Reverse order is 6 through 1 and starts in the actual forward ending state. Track reversibility in the recorded prop, position, and cue states.
works.proof: Run the six-card score forward and immediately in reverse. Publish the script and before/after state at every cue. Use an envelope with a resettable closure and a reversible light or bell indicator if those props change.
works.fixture: A visitor crosses a mark, turns on a cue, opens a flap, removes a key, places it on a bench, and leaves. Require the reverse run to return each object and performer to its initial tracked state. Try one inverse from the wrong prop position and check that it fails.
works.critic: Trace props and marks without a reset between passages. Ask a spectator to describe each passage’s objective and report the earliest cue that loses dramatic or physical continuity.
works.shared: Play E01–E06 straight, then stage the visitor’s return through the reverse chain. Keep the service door closed in both passages.

works.title: One image, two orders of captions
works.byline: Ouvroir de bande dessinée potentielle · Comics
works.line: Repeat one drawing nine times and let two traversal orders change what its captions mean.
works.thesis: Give the eye one stable image and the reader two changing contexts. A line at the center should acquire a different referent or intention according to which captions led to it.
works.state: ◻(Cell) has a coordinate, shared art ID, and immutable lettering. ◻(Route) is an ordered set of nine cell IDs. [read] accumulates a path-local sequence of claims and referents.
works.invariant: Use one drawing at the same crop and scale in every cell. Freeze one caption per cell. Readers traverse the same 3×3 page across rows or down columns. Both routes share their first and last cell. Route labels live outside the panels.
works.proof: Make one nine-panel page and two annotated route transcripts. Give one reading a straightforward report and the other a plausible account of intent. Use the central caption as the hinge and let the shared end close both accounts.
works.fixture: Row order is 11, 12, 13, 21, 22, 23, 31, 32, 33. Column order is 11, 21, 31, 12, 22, 32, 13, 23, 33. Cell 22 follows 21 in the first reading and 12 in the second. Let its caption point to a different established referent in each.
works.critic: Verify plate identity and caption stability across routes. Ask readers to point to the earlier captions that license their different readings of cell 22.
works.shared: Repeat a wide plate of the station bench beneath the closed door. Use the lettering to give one route the incident and the other the suspicion that the key was deliberately left.

works.title: Change one event in the record
works.line: Fork a dated record at one intervention and trace the consequences.
works.thesis: Make a counterfactual expose how much an explanation depends on one event. Retain the archival record as a visible baseline and show the chain each conjecture depends on.
works.state: ◻(Evidence) cites a dated source and proposition. ◻(BaselineEvent) has a time, evidence IDs, and dependencies. [intervene] changes one designated premise. [propagate] adds hypothetical consequences with a named dependency and rationale.
works.invariant: Keep the source ledger intact and behaviors before the fork fixed. Edit exactly one baseline premise at the fork. Keep independent background facts fixed in both timelines. Mark each downstream claim as attested, hypothetical, or unresolved.
works.proof: Make two parallel timelines with five to seven entries each. Show a shared prefix, one mapped change, and at least two downstream steps. Give each divergence a causal predecessor and state what would weaken the inference.
works.fixture: In the fictional station record delay the bell by one minute. Freeze the arrival, objects, and closed door. Give a reason for any changed opening or departure time and show the alternative if the visitor would have acted independently of the bell.
works.critic: Point to the single intervention and reconstruct the proposed chain. Flag silent edits to the baseline and hypothetical inferences presented as sourced evidence.
works.shared: Use the unchanged station record as the baseline and annotate which deductions about the key depend on the bell’s timing.

works.title: A route sampled by the clock
works.line: Make a contact sheet whose exposures follow a fixed interval and route.
works.thesis: Let a clock decide which parts of a place earn a frame. Use blanks, rhythms, and repetitions to show what the walk and camera happened to encounter.
works.state: ◻(Route) has a start, direction, and finish. ◻(Tick) has a scheduled offset, actual capture time, and route position. [expose] records one frame or a missed slot. [contact sheet] preserves the schedule as reading order.
works.invariant: Declare the route, framing policy, six capture times, and tolerance before departure. Take at most one exposure per scheduled time and keep it in its slot. Keep misses visible and record permitted exposure adjustments.
works.proof: Walk one declared segment and build a six-slot contact sheet. Label actual capture time and offset for each frame or a reason for a miss. Include a small route map with the scheduled positions or the actual positions when known.
works.fixture: Schedule offsets 0, 60, 120, 180, 240, and 300 seconds with a two-second tolerance. Simulate a missed 120-second exposure and keep the third position blank. A frame logged at 125 seconds must fail that slot’s timing check.
works.critic: Audit the sequence against capture times and route. Ask what the imposed timing revealed or skipped. Point to each miss and any plausible correction that would alter the rule.
works.shared: Walk the station from entrance to the closed service door. Keep the scheduled third exposure even when the envelope or key sits outside the composition.

works.title: Music that survives a shuffle
works.line: Compose four modules and verify every possible join in a shuffled piece.
works.thesis: Give the listener a continuous pulse when sections change places. Let the same modules make different arcs through register, density, or timbre.
works.state: ◻(Module) has an ID, bar count, tempo, harmonic map, and entry and exit signatures. [join] puts two rendered modules on one beat grid. ◻(Order) uses every ID exactly once.
works.invariant: Freeze four original four-bar modules in one meter, tempo, and boundary harmony. All directed joins between distinct modules must pass the same pulse, harmonic, and audible seam checks. Use identical module renders in both assemblies.
works.proof: Render two audibly distinct orders and a review reel of the twelve directed joins. Include the closing join for each piece if it is presented as a loop. Explain how the same shared motif functions differently in each order.
works.fixture: Use modules A, B, C, and D at 100 bpm in 4/4 with a shared D minor boundary. A–B–C–D and C–A–D–B each have sixteen bars. A one-beat insert at an internal transition must fail the beat-grid check.
works.critic: Listen for dropped beats, harmonic ruptures, cut tails, and indistinct arcs. Verify the full join matrix and mark any seam that needs a new mix or composition.
works.shared: Use four modules keyed to arrival, bell, discovery, and exit, with an original bell pulse as the common motif. Compare what the opening tells the listener to expect.

works.title: Runnable code with an acrostic
works.line: Make one program pass a behavior test and a separate test of its source form.
works.thesis: Give source code two readers. The interpreter receives useful behavior and the human reader can find a message in the names of the functions that perform it.
works.state: ◻(Program) has a language, revision, I/O contract, and execution trace. ◻(Form) gives a syntax-tree selector and target string. [run] tests behavior. [read source] extracts the target letters from declarations.
works.invariant: Freeze the input and output contract before writing. Write six top-level Python function declarations in source order. Their initials must spell a six-letter word. Every function must run on the normal entry path and perform a declared part of the behavior.
works.proof: Deliver one Python program and checks that run it, exercise all six functions, and extract the initials from top-level function declarations with the standard AST parser. Record independent pass or fail results for output and form.
works.fixture: Read an input station record and return its six normalized events in order. Use step_in, echo, access_envelope, locate_key, entrust_bench, and depart so the declarations spell SEALED. Swap two declarations with different initials to fail form alone. Alter an emitted event to fail behavior alone.
works.critic: Run the program from its declared invocation. Check both negative cases and trace every function to a necessary result. Read the source as an acrostic and as maintainable code.
works.shared: Use one function to normalize each of E01–E06. Check the event order and final location of the key in output from the actual entry point.

works.title: An acrostic made with line breaks
works.byline: Potential typography · Typographic and visual poetry
works.line: Keep a text verbatim and use line breaks to reveal a second reading.
works.thesis: Make the eye discover a short second message before or after it reads the full text. Let lineation carry the difference between the two readings.
works.state: ◻(Text) holds an ordered token sequence. ◻(Specimen) declares width, font, and allowed typographic operations. [lineate] maps tokens to rows. [read initials] spells a second message from the start of each designed line.
works.invariant: Use exactly the same characters after normalizing whitespace, in the same order, for both specimens. Lock font family, size, and line height. Allow line breaks, alignment, spacing, and weight.
works.proof: Deliver a run-in specimen and a lineated specimen in which three or more line initials form a readable word. Make the second message enrich the original text. Include a print specimen or a responsive preview that preserves line beginnings in its supported widths.
works.fixture: Use “Keys wait here. Every visitor hears a bell. You will find the door closed.” Break before Every and You to expose K–E–Y. Compare copied text from the two views and test the designed line starts at desktop and 360-pixel widths.
works.critic: Read at the intended distance and identify the primary text and the acrostic. Flag any forced line wrap, clipping, changed text, or secondary reading that requires a legend to notice.
works.shared: Derive a short station notice from E01–E06. Use a second reading to call the eye back to the hidden object.

works.title: Rooms on a knight’s tour
works.line: Distinguish an admissible sequence of rooms from a route that can actually be walked.
works.thesis: Let a formal itinerary reorder how a visitor encounters a building. Test what the geometry and the room program do to a tour that works on a board.
works.state: ◻(Room) has a grid address, program, footprint, and threshold. ◻(Tour) is an ordered room list. [knight move] permits grid offsets (1, 2) or (2, 1) in either direction. [trace] maps each transition to a drawn path.
works.invariant: Visit each room exactly once from entrance to exit. Every consecutive pair makes a legal knight move on room centers. Draw continuous routes that cross only the intended room thresholds in order. Declare any levels and corridor junctions.
works.proof: Produce a twelve-room diagram and a schematic plan. Annotate the walk through all thresholds and mark path crossings and optional choices. Report graph feasibility and drawn walking continuity separately.
works.fixture: Use a 3×4 grid with entrance r1c1 and exit r3c4. A valid address sequence is 11, 23, 31, 12, 24, 32, 13, 21, 33, 14, 22, 34. Check eleven legal moves independently and show an intentional illegal move or repeated room as a failing case.
works.critic: Trace the drawn route without jumping across walls or accidentally entering a future room. Check where the visual or physical experience supports the chosen program sequence.
works.shared: Assign envelope, bell, key, bench, and service threshold to stops on the tour. Use the remaining rooms to control approach and departure.

works.title: Five primitives, two poster hierarchies
works.line: Move the same copy and geometric vocabulary into two different reading orders.
works.thesis: Use placement and scale to change which part of the same message reaches a passerby first. Give the five shapes visual jobs a reader can recognize.
works.state: ◻(Primitive) has a declared geometry type and allowable parameters. ◻(Poster) places labeled, locked copy blocks and shape instances on a fixed grid. [compose] changes scale, placement, repetition, and depth.
works.invariant: Lock the copy, background, palette, font family, weights, and page grid. Use circle, rectangle, triangle, line, and arc as the entire drawn vocabulary apart from fixed text. Each composition must use all five and keep text legible.
works.proof: Make two posters from identical words. Give each a different intended first-read block. Ship editable source and rendered previews, with a legend listing every primitive and its placements.
works.fixture: Set three copy blocks on a 12×18 grid reading “STATION”, “KEY ON BENCH”, and “SERVICE DOOR CLOSED”. Poster A should give the key notice first attention. Poster B should give it to the closed-door notice. Show a primitive audit and compare timed first reads.
works.critic: Before viewing the placements, record the first block you noticed and the action you inferred. Check the shape inventory and inspect legibility at a small viewing scale.
works.shared: Turn the station’s bench, brass key, and shut door into a single recurring mark system. Keep the notice verbatim in both designs.

works.title: Rotate the agenda
works.line: Hold preferences fixed and see which proposals pass when the agenda starts elsewhere.
works.thesis: Make procedural power visible by varying the order in which a body can hear proposals. Show how a time limit changes which votes can occur.
works.state: ◻(Session) has members, fixed ballots, proposal IDs, and allotted slots. [schedule] orders eligible proposals. [truncate] selects the scheduled slots. [tally] calculates adopted proposals from the same ballots and threshold.
works.invariant: Hold proposals, participants, ballots, eligibility, admission time, and decision threshold fixed. Each proposal consumes one equal slot. Compare a fixed queue and a cyclic agenda with only the starting position changed.
works.proof: Simulate four proposals, four voters, and three slots per session. Print both agendas, the order heard, votes cast, resulting decisions, and deferred proposals. Run all four start positions and count who reaches the agenda.
works.fixture: Fix yes totals A=4, B=3, C=2, D=4 and a three-vote threshold. A, B, C yields adopted A and B. D, A, B yields adopted D, A, and B. In a full rotation each proposal is heard in three sessions.
works.critic: Recalculate the outcomes from the disclosed rule. Distinguish ballot support, access to a vote, and adoption. Identify which dependencies would change if participants changed their strategy.
works.shared: Give a fictional station committee four proposals for managing the found key, bench, bell, and service door. Compare two meeting agendas under one time cap.

works.title: One animatic, three ways to see a beat
works.line: Retell six fixed beats by changing movement timing or what the frame lets the viewer see.
works.thesis: Translate Queneau’s repeated incident into animation by making each variation an observable operation on the same action. Let one cut suggest hesitation and another direct attention to incomplete evidence.
works.state: ◻(Incident) has six ordered events and protected facts. ◻(AssetSet) contains shared layers, poses, and sound. ◻(Animatic) has an exposure sheet and viewing rectangle. [retime] changes holds and transitions. [reframe] changes the visible field.
works.invariant: Lock the rigs or artwork, protected key poses, props, event order, sound bed, and 288-frame runtime at 24 fps. The timing variant changes holds and transitions while keeping the baseline frame. The framing variant keeps the baseline exposure sheet and uses one altered viewing rectangle.
works.proof: Render a baseline and two twelve-second animatics. In the timing variant lengthen anticipation before the envelope opens and pay back the frames elsewhere. In the framing variant limit peripheral visibility and give each protected action a cue within the smaller field.
works.fixture: Start with six windows of 48 frames. Give the timing branch window lengths 36, 36, 72, 48, 48, and 48. In the framing branch preserve the six original event windows and use one fixed crop chosen from the baseline stage. Count decoded frames and log concrete visual cues for E01–E06 in all three exports.
works.critic: Watch each clip once before consulting the cue map. Identify all six actions and the strongest perceived shift in expectation. Check that the crop preserves visible evidence and that the timing branch drew its evidence from the same poses.
works.shared: Hold on the closed envelope before E03 to change the visitor’s apparent intent. Try a restricted window centered on the handoff to the bench and make the door’s closure legible in all cuts.
